content: Hormone replacement therapy (HRT), which includes estrogen and progestin, may increase the risk of serious health conditions such as heart attack, stroke, breast cancer, and blood clots in the lungs and legs. It is crucial to inform your doctor if you smoke or if you have a history of breast lumps or cancer, heart attack, stroke, blood clots, high blood pressure, high cholesterol or fat levels, or diabetes. If you are scheduled for surgery or will be on bed rest, consult your doctor about discontinuing estrogen and progestin at least 4-6 weeks prior to the procedure or period of inactivity. If you experience any of the following symptoms, contact your doctor immediately: sudden and severe headache, sudden and severe vomiting, sudden partial or complete loss of vision, speech problems, dizziness or faintness, weakness or numbness in an arm or leg, crushing chest pain or chest heaviness, coughing up blood, sudden shortness of breath, or calf pain. Discuss the risks and benefits of taking estrogen and progestin with your doctor. Estrogen and progestin combinations are prescribed to treat specific symptoms of menopause. Estrogen and progestin are female sex hormones. HRT works by replacing estrogen that the body no longer produces. Estrogen helps reduce hot flashes, vaginal symptoms (such as itching, burning, and dryness), and urinary difficulties, but it does not alleviate other menopause symptoms like nervousness or depression. Estrogen also helps prevent bone thinning (osteoporosis) in menopausal women. Progestin is added to estrogen in HRT to lower the risk of uterine cancer in women who still have their uterus. HRT is available as an oral tablet, typically taken once daily. To ensure consistency, take it at the same time every day. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take the medication exactly as directed, without altering the dose or frequency. Do not stop taking the medication without consulting your doctor. Specific HRT products include Activella, FemHRT, and Prempro, which are taken as one tablet daily. Ortho-Prefest comes in a blister card with 30 tablets; take one pink tablet (containing only estrogen) daily for 3 days, followed by one white tablet (containing estrogen and progestin) daily for 3 days, and repeat this cycle until the card is finished. Start a new blister card the day after completing the previous one. Premphase comes in a dispenser with 28 tablets; take one maroon tablet (containing only estrogen) daily for days 1-14, and one light-blue tablet (containing estrogen and progestin) daily for days 15-28. Begin a new dispenser the day after finishing the last one. Before starting HRT, ask your pharmacist or doctor for the manufacturer’s patient information and read it carefully. This medication may also be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before taking HRT, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to estrogen, progestin, or any other medications. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Mention specific medications such as acetaminophen, anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), cyclosporine, seizure medications (e.g., carbamazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin), morphine, oral steroids (e.g., dexamethasone, prednisone), rifampin, salicylic acid, temazepam, theophylline, and thyroid medications (e.g., levothyroxine). Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you for side effects. Additionally, inform your doctor if you have had a hysterectomy or if you have a history of asthma, toxemia (high blood pressure during pregnancy), depression, epilepsy, migraine headaches, liver, heart, gallbladder, or kidney disease, jaundice, vaginal bleeding between menstrual periods, or excessive weight gain and fluid retention during the menstrual cycle. Notify your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you become pregnant while taking this medication, contact your doctor immediately, as estrogen and progestin may harm the fetus. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental surgery, inform your doctor or dentist that you are taking HRT. Let your doctor know if you smoke, as smoking while on this medication increases the risk of serious side effects like blood clots and stroke. Smoking may also reduce the effectiveness of the medication. If you wear contact lenses, inform your doctor and pharmacist. If you notice changes in vision or difficulty wearing your lenses while on HRT, consult an eye doctor. Ask your doctor about taking calcium supplements if you are using this medication to prevent osteoporosis. Follow all dietary and exercise recommendations, as these can help prevent bone disease. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. HRT may cause side effects. Inform your doctor if any of the following symptoms are severe or persistent: headache, upset stomach, vomiting, stomach cramps or bloating, diarrhea, appetite and weight changes, changes in sex drive or ability, nervousness, brown or black skin patches, acne, swelling of hands, feet, or lower legs (fluid retention), bleeding or spotting between menstrual periods, changes in menstrual flow, breast tenderness, enlargement, or discharge, or difficulty wearing contact lenses. Some side effects can be serious. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience double vision, severe abdominal pain, yellowing of the skin or eyes, severe mental depression, unusual bleeding, loss of appetite, rash, extreme tiredness, weakness, lack of energy, fever, dark-colored urine, or light-colored stool. HRT may increase the risk of endometrial cancer and gallbladder disease. Discuss these risks with your doctor. Report any unusual problems while taking this medication to your doctor. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store this medication in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Dispose of outdated or unneeded medication properly. Consult your pharmacist for disposal instructions. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the victim has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911. Symptoms of overdose may include upset stomach and vomiting. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory. You should have a complete physical exam, including blood pressure measurements, breast and pelvic exams, and a Pap test at least once a year. Follow your doctor’s instructions for breast self-exams and report any lumps immediately. If you are taking HRT for menopause symptoms, your doctor will reassess every 3-6 months to determine if you still need the medication. If you are taking it to prevent osteoporosis, you may need to use it for a longer period. Inform laboratory personnel that you are taking HRT, as it may interfere with certain tests. Do not share your medication with others. Consult your pharmacist with any questions about refilling your prescription.
